lessons.subject: physics
lessons.title: Measurements and Units
lessons.html:
Measurements and Units

A physical quantity is a measurable property expressed by a numerical value and a unit. SI fundamental quantities include length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity. Derived quantities are combinations of fundamental quantities; for example force has unit kg m s−2 and pressure has unit kg m−1s−2.

Measurement

A metre rule measures ordinary lengths. A vernier caliper measures internal and external dimensions and depth with greater precision. A micrometer screw gauge is suitable for small diameters and thicknesses. A beam balance measures mass and a stopwatch measures time. Instrument zero error and limited resolution affect measurements.

Dimensions

Dimensions express a physical quantity in terms of fundamental quantities. Velocity has dimension LT−1, acceleration LT−2, force MLT−2, pressure ML−1T−2 and energy ML2T−2. A valid physical equation must be dimensionally homogeneous.

Distance and displacement

Distance is total path length and is scalar. Displacement is directed change in position and is vector. Measurements should be recorded with suitable significant figures and, when appropriate, in standard form.

lessons.subject: physics
lessons.title: Scalars and Vectors
lessons.html:
Scalars and Vectors

A scalar has magnitude only, while a vector has magnitude and direction. Mass, time, distance, speed, energy and temperature are scalars. Displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and momentum are vectors.

Vector operations

Vectors may be added geometrically using the triangle or parallelogram law. A vector F at angle θ to the x-axis has components Fx=F cosθ and Fy=F sinθ. The magnitude of the resultant of perpendicular components is √(Fx²+Fy²).

Relative velocity is obtained by vector subtraction. The velocity of A relative to B is vA/B=vA−vB. Careful choice of positive direction is essential.

lessons.subject: physics
lessons.title: Motion
lessons.html:
Motion

Motion is change of position with time relative to a reference frame. Speed is distance per unit time and velocity is displacement per unit time. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.

Uniformly accelerated motion

For constant acceleration, v=u+at, s=ut+½at² and v²=u²+2as. The gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration and the area under it gives displacement.

Projectile and circular motion

Projectile motion is resolved into independent horizontal and vertical components. Neglecting air resistance, horizontal acceleration is zero and vertical acceleration is g downward. Circular motion requires centripetal acceleration v²/r and centripetal force mv²/r.

Momentum and SHM

Momentum p=mv and impulse is change in momentum. In an isolated system total momentum is conserved. In simple harmonic motion, acceleration is proportional to displacement and directed toward equilibrium. Resonance occurs when a driving frequency approaches a natural frequency.

lessons.subject: physics
lessons.title: Gravity
lessons.html:
Gravity

Gravitation is the attractive interaction between masses. Newton's universal law gives F=Gm1m2/r². Near Earth's surface, weight W=mg.

Mass is the amount of matter and is measured in kilograms. Weight is a force measured in newtons and changes with gravitational field strength. The gravitational field strength produced by a point mass is g=GM/r².

Satellites remain in orbit because gravitational attraction supplies the required centripetal force. As distance from the attracting body's centre increases, gravitational field strength decreases.

lessons.subject: physics
lessons.title: Equilibrium of Forces
lessons.html:
Equilibrium of Forces

A body is in translational equilibrium when the vector sum of all forces is zero. For coplanar forces, horizontal and vertical components must each balance.

Moments and couples

The moment of a force about a point is M=Fd, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. A couple consists of equal, opposite parallel forces and has turning moment equal to one force multiplied by the perpendicular separation.

Lami's theorem and stability

For three concurrent forces in equilibrium, Lami's theorem gives F1/sinα=F2/sinβ=F3/sinγ. A stable body develops a restoring tendency after a small displacement; an unstable body moves farther away, while neutral equilibrium leaves it in the new position.

lessons.html:
Friction

Friction is a contact force opposing relative motion or its tendency. Static friction acts before sliding and has a limiting value μN; kinetic friction acts during sliding. Friction is useful for traction and braking but causes wear and energy loss. Lubricants and rolling bearings reduce unwanted friction.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic Induction
lessons.html:
Electromagnetic Induction

Changing magnetic flux linkage induces emf. Faraday's law relates induced emf to the rate of change of flux linkage and Lenz's law determines direction. Generators and transformers depend on electromagnetic induction.

lessons.title: Simple A. C. Circuits
lessons.html:
Simple A. C. Circuits

Alternating current changes direction periodically. For a sinusoid v=V0sinωt and Vrms=V0/√2. In a resistor current and voltage are in phase; in an inductor current lags and in a capacitor current leads. XL=2πfL and XC=1/(2πfC).

lessons.title: Conduction of Electricity Through
lessons.html:
Conduction of Electricity Through

Metals conduct through free electrons; electrolytes through ions; ionized gases through charged particles. Electrolysis produces chemical changes through current. Faraday's laws relate deposited material to electric charge.

lessons.title: Elementary Modern Physics
lessons.html:
Elementary Modern Physics

Modern physics includes atomic energy levels, spectra, photoelectric emission, X-rays and radioactivity. Photon energy is E=hf. Einstein's photoelectric equation is hf=φ+Kmax. Half-life describes radioactive decay. Nuclear fission and fusion involve changes in nuclear binding energy.

lessons.subject: physics
lessons.title: Introductory Electronics
lessons.html:
Introductory Electronics

Semiconductors have conductivity between conductors and insulators. Intrinsic semiconductors are pure; doping produces n-type and p-type materials. Diodes are p-n junction devices used for rectification. Transistors are three-terminal devices used for amplification and switching.
